query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Vacuum infiltration of the brittle (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy with a ductile Zn-based metallic binder at moderate temperature will increase bulk mechanical integrity and maintain comparable caloric performance to the unreinforced compound.
generation.material_initial_state: A cast and consolidated (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy magnetocaloric alloy prone to cracking under stress.
generation.intervention: Introduce a low-melting Zn-based metallic phase by vacuum-assisted infiltration at 400–600 K across the alloy’s porous network, forming a composite microstructure.
generation.conditions: Ambient to ~400–600 K infiltration temperature under partial vacuum, followed by applied magnetic fields up to ~2 T and moderate barocaloric loads (pressures of similar magnitude to prior mechanical tests).
generation.structural_mediator: A thin, continuous metallic binder phase occupying preexisting microcracks and intergranular gaps, solidified in situ.
generation.mechanism: The ductile Zn-based infiltrant bridges grain boundaries, reducing crack formation and enhancing thermal conductivity, while leaving the magnetocaloric phase continuity and active volume largely intact.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compressive strength increases by at least tens of MPa relative to the unreinforced alloy (comparable to or exceeding epoxy-based strengths), with minimal loss (<10%) in magnetic/pressure-driven caloric response. Thermal conductivity is also improved over epoxy-infiltrated analogs.
generation.baseline: Unreinforced (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 showing cracking and low compressive strength with only partial success from prior epoxy or In-based infiltration methods.
generation.boundary: Infiltration must fully wet grain boundaries without dissolving or reacting with the magnetostructural phases; infiltration void must be minimized to ensure improved mechanical continuity. Excess infiltration temperature or time risks altering the parent phase and diminishing caloric performance.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative gains in compressive strength and heat transfer are not fully established without further experiment.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples, one unreinforced and the other vacuum-infiltrated with Zn-based alloy at 400–600 K. Verify infiltration quality by microscopy. Conduct compressive strength tests, thermal conductivity measurements, and magnetocaloric performance tests (ΔT and ΔS under ~2 T). Compare the reinforced composite performance to the baseline unreinforced samples.
measurements: Compressive strength (MPa) before and after infiltration
Thermal conductivity (W/mK) of the composite vs. unreinforced alloy
Magnetocaloric temperature and entropy changes at ~2 T
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the infiltrated alloy does not exhibit stronger compressive strength than the baseline or if caloric performance degrades by more than ~10%, the hypothesis is falsified.

chosen.technique: pressure-assisted infiltration with a low-melting Zn-based alloy

chosen.why: Employing a zinc-based metallic infiltration can form a robust composite matrix that simultaneously increases mechanical strength and thermal conductivity. Because the magnetocaloric phase is retained and remains rare-earth-free, the caloric response is preserved. Prior work with other low-melting infiltrants confirms that infiltration can enhance structural integrity without sacrificing functional properties, and a simple vacuum infiltration followed by compression testing would confirm this hypothesis or falsify it if the composite fails to maintain both adequate strength and caloric output.
